title: Lattice Corneal Dystrophy: The Amyloid Network
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Lattice Corneal Dystrophy (LCD), an autosomal dominant TGFBI-linked amyloidosis. This poster details the classification, histopathology, and multi-modal management of one of the most common stromal dystrophies.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Lattice Corneal Dystrophy (LCD) is the most common form of stromal corneal dystrophy characterized by the deposition of amyloid fibrils within the corneal stroma. It is primarily an autosomal dominant condition associated with mutations in the TGFBI gene (Transforming Growth Factor Beta Induced) on chromosome 5q31. Clinically, it presents with branching, refractile lattice lines, subepithelial white dots, and a progressive stromal haze, often leading to recurrent corneal erosions (RCE) and significant visual impairment by the fourth or fifth decade of life.

sections.title: Clinical Features: The Slit-Lamp Exam
content: Fine, branching, refractile lines in the anterior/mid stroma.
Small, white subepithelial dots (amyloid deposits).
Diffuse stromal haze (ground-glass appearance) in later stages.
Lattice lines usually clear the peripheral 1-2mm (limbal sparing).
Recurrent Corneal Erosions (RCE) often precede lattice lines.
Decreased corneal sensitivity due to nerve involvement/amyloid.

sections.title: Red Flags: Meretoja Syndrome (LCD Type II)
content: Progressive Cranial Nerve Palsies (esp. Facial Nerve VII)
Mask-like facies (due to facial nerve involvement)
Cutis Laxa (loose, redundant skin)
Peripheral Neuropathy
Cardiac Arrhythmias or Amyloid Cardiomyopathy
Autonomic dysfunction (Postural hypotension)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. High-Magnification Slit-Lamp: Retroillumination is key for refractile lines.
2. Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT): Visualizes hyperreflective stromal deposits and epithelial irregularities.
3. In Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM): Shows highly reflective, branching linear structures in the stroma.
4. Genetic Testing: TGFBI gene sequencing for definitive typing.
5. Corneal Sensitivity (Cochet-Bonnet): Often reduced early on.

rows: Diffuse haze to limbus, thinning, Autosomal Recessive
Central subepithelial crystals, arcus senilis early
Combination of granular dots and lattice lines

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1: Conservative management of RCE (Lubricants, Hypertonic saline, Bandage Contact Lens).
Step 2: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) for superficial deposits and RCE prevention.
Step 3: Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) if deposits are deep but endothelium is healthy.
Step 4: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) for full-thickness stromal haze.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring for recurrence (Common in LCD).

rows: High success; risk of graft rejection

content.mnemonic: Marilyn Monroe Got Hers in Los Angeles
content.explanation: Macular = Mucopolysaccharide; Granular = Hyaline; Lattice = Amyloid.

sections.title: Prognosis & Recurrence
content: Lattice has the highest recurrence rate among stromal dystrophies.
Recurrence in graft usually occurs within 3-10 years post-op.
Recurrent deposits often start as a peripheral subepithelial haze.
Secondary RCE can occur even after successful keratoplasty.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: LCD Type I is almost always TGFBI Arg124Cys.
In retroillumination, lattice lines look like 'glass threads'.
Vision loss is dual-mode: chronic haze + acute RCE episodes.
Decreased corneal sensation is a helpful diagnostic sign for LCD.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Data
sections.content: Recent research focuses on siRNA (small interfering RNA) to silence the mutant TGFBI allele and gene editing via CRISPR/Cas9. Studies have shown that DALK may offer better long-term outcomes than PKP for LCD because the amyloid deposits do not involve the host endothelium, and maintaining the host's own endothelium reduces the long-term risk of rejection. However, recurrence in the donor stroma remains a significant hurdle across all keratoplasty techniques.
